source: Perttula & Liikkanen (2006) Exposure effects in design idea generation: unconscious conformity or a product of sampling probability? NordDesign
finding: Sixteen mechanical engineering students got four heterogeneous example designs or none for a plant-watering task. Examples did not raise how often example features reappeared. They did cut the number of new solution categories explored. The authors read this as a sampling-probability effect (examples use up the easy ideas) rather than unconscious conformity.
numbers: N=16 (8 per group), 20 min, between subjects. Ideas: 9.38 (SD 4.07) exposure vs 8.75 (SD 2.31) control, p=.75. Categories: 12.88 vs 13.00, p=.96. Non-redundant categories: 6.00 (SD 2.00) vs 13.00 (SD 4.54), t=3.74, p=.01 (about 50% fewer). All 12 example-category frequencies and explicit-linkage rates not significant (e.g. separate tank .55 vs .47, p=.50; total explicit links .64 vs .57, p=.48).
limits: Tiny N. The non-redundant-category row is odd (control equals its own total of 13), so the metric looks asymmetric. Four varied examples, instructed not to copy, 20 minutes: a setup unlike Jansson and Smith (one example, flawed features, short time). Authors list five reasons for the mismatch.
agent_relevance: Under-exploring an example's own territory is not the same as copying it. A fresh context that never saw the example avoids both. Measure category coverage, not only copied features.

source: Perttula & Liikkanen (2006) Exposure effects in design idea generation: unconscious conformity or a product of sampling probability? NordDesign (review section: Jansson and Smith 1991 as summarised)
finding: Jansson and Smith: half the subjects saw one pictured example before design; example features stayed at an abnormal rate in their designs. Replicated across four design problems, also in experienced designers, and also when the copied features were flawed.
numbers: Four design problems (second-hand; exact N and percentages not read in the original).
limits: Second-hand via the opened review; original not opened this session. Total output was only about 3 to 4 ideas per subject, so effect on later ideas is unknown.
agent_relevance: Founding effect is about the first few ideas. Our S3 fresh contexts target exactly that early window.

source: Perttula & Liikkanen (2006) Exposure effects in design idea generation: unconscious conformity or a product of sampling probability? NordDesign (review section: Smith, Ward and Schumacher; Purcell and Gero)
finding: Smith et al. (1993) found in three experiments that examples constrain features of new toys and imaginary creatures. Purcell and colleagues found fixation only when the example held principles that are part of the designer's own expertise, mostly at an abstract conceptual level, and reproduction was highest for statistically common ideas.
numbers: Three experiments for Smith et al. (second-hand). No numbers reported in the review.
limits: Second-hand. Purcell, Williams and Gero (1993) reported weak replication; see the next line.
agent_relevance: Fixation tracks familiarity and typicality. A language model's most familiar answer acts like its own example, so the model may be fixated before any context is added.

source: Purcell, Williams & Gero (1993) Fixation effects: do they exist in design problem solving? Environment and Planning B
finding: Search-result snippet only: attempts to replicate Jansson and Smith were largely unsuccessful, and apparent fixation was tied to familiarity with existing solutions to the problem. Treat as unverified until the paper is read.
numbers: Not read. No numbers.
limits: Only a snippet. The 2006 Perttula review says Purcell found effects only with expertise-relevant examples.
agent_relevance: A failed or conditional replication in the founding line. Do not assume the effect is universal.

source: Perttula & Liikkanen (2006) Exposure effects in design idea generation: unconscious conformity or a product of sampling probability? NordDesign (review section: sampling-probability experiment and stimulation)
finding: In an earlier experiment by the same authors, examples given up front versus after 20 minutes: those given up front covered significantly fewer solution categories. Examples can also stimulate new ideas, but that did not outweigh the negative effect in past studies.
numbers: Second-hand; no figures. In the opened study, 13 explicit cases where an example triggered a new sub-function solution, 27% of 47 extra solutions.
limits: Timing manipulation cited, not read directly.
agent_relevance: Order matters: introducing examples late preserves diversity. Supports generating own ideas first, then retrieving.

source: Neroni, Vasconcelos & Crilly (2017) Studying design fixation with a computer-based task. ICED17
finding: Fixation shown as a Luchins-style mental set in a bridge-design game with an objective cost measure. Engineers first given five single-approach trials kept using the costlier approach on later trials where a cheaper one was possible. The fixating solution came from their own first experience, not from a supplied example.
numbers: N=40 recruited, 36 analysed, 18 per group. Participants using the costlier all-anchor approach in dual-approach trials: 15 (83%) vs 8 (44%), chi2(1)=5.90, p=.01, phi=.40. Trials solved that way: 34 (47%) vs 13 (18%), chi2=13.93, phi=.31. Total cost: $30,077 (SD 2,701) vs $27,461 (SD 2,000), t(34)=3.3, p=.002, d=1.10. Time per trial 102 vs 74 s, d=.70. First tested design cost, d=1.06.
limits: Cambridge engineering students, one task, order manipulation only. Not an example-exposure test. Authors say it is closer to mental set than to functional fixedness.
agent_relevance: Self-made fixation: the agent's own first successful approach can lock later work. A new context drops the earlier trials, which is what the control group effectively had.

source: Neroni et al. (2017), as reported: Luchins water-jar mental set
finding: Luchins: after a run of problems solved by one long method, most people kept the long method on a problem with a one-step solution. A control group seeing only the critical problem solved it fast. Described second-hand.
numbers: No numbers given in the secondary text.
limits: Second-hand; original not opened.
agent_relevance: Direct support for the claim that a run of similar prior steps in one context raises fixation, and a clean context resets it.

source: Neroni et al. (2017), as reported: Jansson and Smith instruction result
finding: Per the secondary text, Jansson and Smith found the repetition of example features persisted even when participants were told to avoid copying those features.
numbers: Not given. Problems: car bicycle rack, measuring cup for the blind, spill-proof coffee cup.
limits: Second-hand; original not opened. Contrast with Perttula (2006) where the instruction not to copy coincided with no copying.
agent_relevance: A prompt line saying 'do not copy the example' cannot be trusted to work. Removing the example (S3) is the safer control.

source: Neroni et al. (2017), as reported: review landscape
finding: The paper names three reviews of design fixation: Youmans and Arciszewski (2014, concepts), Sio, Kotovsky and Cagan (2015, findings, a meta-analytic review) and Vasconcelos and Crilly (2016, methods). It says existing studies are methodologically homogeneous: open-ended early ideation, subjective metrics.
numbers: No effect sizes in this text. Sio et al. full text was not obtainable this session (publisher page only redirected).
limits: Sio meta-analysis numbers still missing; flagged as a gap.
agent_relevance: The human evidence base rests on short ideation tasks with human-rated scores. Treat transfer to agents as a hypothesis.

source: Deng, Brucks & Toubia (2026) Examining and Addressing Barriers to Diversity in LLM-Generated Ideas. arXiv:2602.20408
finding: Study 1: LLM sessions show about the same within-session fixation as humans (ten sequential fitness-product ideas), but far less diversity across sessions. So fixation is not the main reason LLM pools are narrow; lack of knowledge partitioning across 'people' is.
numbers: Humans N=99 (Prolific), simulated LLM participants N=99. Per participant: categories 12.68 vs 12.46, combinations 8.37 vs 8.68 (p=.12), pairwise distance 2.10 vs 2.11 (p=.78); accumulation slopes 1.035 vs 1.013 (p=.51). Pooled 99 sessions: categories 28 vs 22, unique combinations 206 vs 88. Groups of 10, first-idea pairwise distance 2.41 vs 1.51.
limits: One task (fitness products), one set of LLMs, category coding by an LLM pipeline. Fixation measured as slope of diversity within a session.
agent_relevance: Within one context, the agent is as fixated as a person. The big loss is across contexts. Fresh contexts only help if each one is also pushed to a different region (personas, seeds).

source: Deng, Brucks & Toubia (2026), Study 2 (human first-idea seeding)
finding: Giving each LLM session a different human-written first idea as a seed did nothing for later diversity.
numbers: Ideas 2 to 10 compared. Categories: default 18.34 vs seeded 18.35 (p=.95). Combinations 38.22 vs 38.16 (p=.89). Pairwise distance 2.07 vs 2.07 (p=.49). N=99 per arm.
limits: Seed was a single idea; other seed types untested. Single domain.
agent_relevance: An example seed is a weak lever in models too. Persona or role cues were what worked.

source: Deng, Brucks & Toubia (2026), Study 3 (personas)
finding: Ordinary personas (everyday people) raised cross-session diversity to near human level. 'Creative entrepreneur' personas helped less. But ordinary personas increased within-session fixation versus default.
numbers: N=99 sessions per arm. Totals: default 22 categories, 83 combinations; ordinary persona 27 categories and 193 combinations vs human 28 and 197. Entrepreneur: 22.98 categories, 50.40 combinations vs default 18.45, 39.15 (bootstrapped); persona 24.02, 56.97. Pairwise distance persona 2.36, entrepreneur 2.28, default 2.04.
limits: Persona fixation measured by slope; the fixation cost is a trade-off.
agent_relevance: Different starting frames across fresh contexts work, but each frame can lock its own context. Pair frames with an intra-context breaker.

source: Deng, Brucks & Toubia (2026), Study 4 (chain-of-thought)
finding: Chain-of-thought ideation (list 10 short titles, then revise to be bolder and more different) cut LLM fixation and raised diversity. The same instruction did not help humans and slightly hurt them. CoT plus ordinary personas gave the highest diversity, above humans.
numbers: N=83 per arm after sampling. Total categories / unique combinations: Human 28/197; Human CoT 28/193; LLM default 22/83; LLM+CoT 27/152; LLM persona CoT 27/248 (26% above human on combinations).
limits: Batch generation differs from the sequential default, so CoT and batching are confounded; the authors ran a sequential robustness check with a smaller gain. Human CoT arm lost 16 of 99 to an attention filter.
agent_relevance: Humans cannot obey 'think differently'; models can. Instructions that restructure the generation are a legitimate lever for an agent.

source: Meincke, Mollick & Terwiesch (2024) Prompting Diverse Ideas: Increasing AI Idea Variance. Wharton working paper (arXiv:2402.01727)
finding: GPT-4 idea pools are less diverse than human group pools. Prompt engineering narrows the gap; chain-of-thought gives the most diversity of the 35 prompts. Persona, 'think like Steve Jobs', and article-based prompts help little.
numbers: Cosine similarity: human groups about 0.243, GPT-4 prompts 0.255 to 0.432, base prompt 0.377 to 0.386, Steve Jobs 0.368. Pools of 1000 ideas per strategy (10 x 100). Estimated idea space: about 3700 unique ideas for base, about 4700 for CoT; repeats 13.8% vs 11.7%. Differences significant at p<.01 by bootstrap and permutation.
limits: One domain (student product under $50), one model (GPT-4), cosine similarity on embeddings is a coarse measure; working paper.
agent_relevance: Diversity is gained by changing the process (list, then differentiate), not by naming an expert.

source: Meincke et al. (2024), seeding and overlap findings
finding: Pools from different prompting strategies overlap little in their first 50 ideas, so combining strategies gives more spread than running one strategy more times. Prompting with seven prior top ideas did not make the pool much more diverse.
numbers: First 50 ideas per pool compared. 'Previous Top Ideas' pool cosine about 0.403 vs base about 0.386 (read from the strategy table).
limits: Reading values off a table layout; exact row alignment slightly uncertain.
agent_relevance: Give-an-example prompting is not a diversity tool in models either. Mix strategies across fresh contexts.

source: Anderson, Shah & Kreminski (2024) Homogenization Effects of LLMs on Human Creative Ideation. C&C 2024 (arXiv:2402.01536)
finding: Within-subject test of ChatGPT versus the Oblique Strategies deck for divergent ideation. ChatGPT users produced more ideas and more categories, with no sign of added fixation within a person, but ideas across people were more alike.
numbers: N=36, tasks counterbalanced. Group-level similarity to the mean embedding higher with ChatGPT: t(32)=3.21, p=.003, d=.67. Individual-level diversity not different (.65 vs .66, p=.35). Ideas: 8.39 (SD 3.39) with ChatGPT, about 15% more. Categories 8.58 vs 6.77, t(32)=3.50, p=.001, d=.54. Elaboration d=.32 (p=.044).
limits: Small N, convenience sample, one task type, embedding-based similarity validated only in a small check. Quality of ideas not rated.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as Deng: tool-assisted sets are individually fine but collectively narrow. Fixation shows at the pool level.

source: Doshi & Hauser (2024) Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content. Science Advances
finding: Preregistered experiment: writers given 0, 1 or up to 5 GPT-4 story-starting ideas. Stories with AI ideas rated more novel and useful, most for less creative writers, but stories were more alike each other, and moved toward the AI idea (anchoring).
numbers: 293 stories, 600 evaluators, 3519 ratings. Novelty +5.4% (b=.207, p=.021) with one idea; +8.1% (b=.311, p<.001) with five. Usefulness +3.7% and +9.0%. Low-creativity writers: novelty +6.3% and +10.7%, usefulness +5.5% and +11.5%. Between-story similarity rose by amounts equal to 10.7% and 8.9% of the human-only similarity range (8.10 points).
limits: Single short-story task; the AI idea was optional to use; effect on novelty is modest and similarity is embedding-based.
agent_relevance: An outside example both helps quality and narrows the set. A mild example may help a weak solver and hurt a strong one. A rule for when to show a hint.

source: Doshi & Hauser (2024), moderator: individual creativity
finding: Benefit from outside ideas was larger for writers with low scores on the Divergent Association Task. The gain for high scorers was smaller.
numbers: DAT mean 77.24, SD 6.48 (N=291 scored). Low-DAT novelty +6.3% (one idea) and +10.7% (five), versus +5.4% and +8.1% overall.
limits: Subgroup split is not a causal moderator test.
agent_relevance: A strong solver gains little from a hint and may be pulled off course. Gate hints on how weak the first attempt is.

source: Padmakumar & He (2024) Does writing with language models reduce content diversity? ICLR 2024 (arXiv:2309.05196)
finding: Controlled study of essay writing with no model, a base model (GPT-3), or a feedback-tuned model (InstructGPT). Only InstructGPT reduced diversity and raised similarity between authors; the base model did not.
numbers: 38 writers from Upwork. Queries about 9.15 per essay; acceptance rate about 70%; model-written text about 32% (InstructGPT). Homogenization significantly higher for InstructGPT than Solo and GPT-3 (t-tests, 5% level).
limits: Argumentative essays, not ideation; small writer pool; the link to fixation is by analogy.
agent_relevance: Alignment tuning is a cause of the narrowing. A moderator: the same suggestions do nothing with a base model. Our model's tuning may set how strongly a hint fixes.

source: Padmakumar & He (2024), diversity metrics detail
finding: Homogenization of an essay was defined as its average pairwise similarity to other essays on the same topic, with two metrics (BERT-score based and key-point overlap). The effect came from the model's suggested key points.
numbers: Metrics range 0 to 1. Writers accepted about 70% of suggestions; about 35% of characters in each essay came from the model.
limits: Metrics validated against human similarity ratings only indirectly.
agent_relevance: A cheap scoring recipe for our own tests: average pairwise similarity of final answers across fresh contexts.

source: Jiang et al. (2025/2026) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models. arXiv:2510.22954
finding: 26K real open-ended queries, 70+ models. Even at high temperature or with min-p sampling, one model repeats itself, and different models give near-identical answers to open questions.
numbers: Same-model pairwise similarity above 0.8 in 79% of cases (Figure 4 text). Cross-model average pairwise similarity 71% to 82%; DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82; DeepSeek-V3 vs gpt-4o 0.81. Min-p, temperature 2.0: still above 0.8. 31,250 human annotations.
limits: Sentence-embedding similarity (text-embedding-3-small) can overstate sameness; read from the paper text, not rechecked against the data.
agent_relevance: Resampling the same model in fresh contexts, or switching to another model, gives little new. Diversity needs prompt-level changes, not temperature and not a different vendor.

source: Si, Yang & Hashimoto (2024/25) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? arXiv:2409.04109
finding: Generating thousands of ideas per topic gives mostly repeats. Only about 5% of 4000 seed ideas survived deduplication at cosine 0.8, with the non-duplicate count plateauing near 200.
numbers: 4000 seed ideas per topic; about 5% non-duplicates; about 200 accumulated non-duplicates (Figure 4). 79 expert reviewers from 32 institutions rated ideas elsewhere in the paper.
limits: Dedup threshold 0.8 was chosen by manual inspection. NLP research topics only.
agent_relevance: More samples in the same setup hit a wall fast. A fresh context must change something real to add new ideas.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI. arXiv:2502.05870
finding: Qualitative study: ten novice designers designed chairs with ChatGPT and Midjourney in a 30 minute session. Most noticed repetition. The paper offers a framework of causes (data bias, architecture, prompting) and mitigations, not a controlled measurement.
numbers: N=10. Seven noticed repetition in ChatGPT output and eight in Midjourney. Participants named repeated terms such as 'modular', 'adaptive', 'ergonomics'. 3 of 10 asked ChatGPT for the first idea.
limits: No control group, no effect size, novices only. Evidence is interview self-report plus observation.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence that models fixate on stock phrases. Useful as a list of failure signatures to detect, not as a measured effect.

source: Deng et al. (2026) with Meincke et al. (2024): rival explanations compared
finding: Two rival explanations for LLM narrowness: (1) within-session fixation (early outputs constrain later ones), (2) lack of knowledge partitioning across samples (every run draws on the same distribution). The data discriminate: within-session fixation equals humans, cross-session spread differs, so (2) dominates; CoT addresses (1), personas address (2).
numbers: Study 1 within-session slope 1.035 human vs 1.013 LLM (p=.51); between-session first-idea distance 2.41 vs 1.51.
limits: The discriminating test uses a single task and one embedding measure.
agent_relevance: Pick the lever by the failure: restructure a session for in-session fixation, vary the starting frame across sessions for sameness.

source: Perttula & Liikkanen (2006), moderator argument
finding: The authors list reasons the Jansson and Smith effect may vanish: several varied examples instead of one, more total ideas (fixation strongest early), larger solution space, an explicit instruction not to copy, and hidden latent attributes not measured.
numbers: Earlier work they cite had about 3 to 4 ideas per subject; their subjects gave about 9. Source-monitoring studies (Landau) are cited as showing that keeping examples visible cut conformity.
limits: Author speculation, not tested in that paper.
agent_relevance: Boundary conditions to test on the agent: one example vs several, early vs late ideas, with vs without a 'do not copy' line.

source: Si et al. (2024/25) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? (headline claim)
finding: The paper's headline is that LLM ideas are rated more novel than expert human ideas, with a lack of diversity. Only the duplication analysis and abstract-level claims were looked at this session.
numbers: 79 reviewers from 32 institutions (read); other figures not extracted.
limits: Headline claim not checked against the tables.
agent_relevance: High average quality with low variance: a pool-level problem rather than a per-answer problem.

source: Anderson et al. (2024), interaction moderators
finding: How people used ChatGPT did not change the sameness: starting with own ideas or with the model, unusual prompts or copied prompts all gave the same homogeneity. About 86% pasted the task prompt directly.
numbers: Own-ideas-first vs LLM-first: ideas 8.38 vs 8.71 (p=.784); homogeneity .99 vs .99. Unusual vs copied prompt: .99 vs .99 (p=.927). 31 of 36 (86.11%) copy-pasted the prompt; 26 (72.22%) iterated.
limits: Within-user comparisons with small cells.
agent_relevance: Order of own thinking vs the model's did not matter here, which cuts against 'think first, then look' as a fix in this setup.
